examples.whatToDo: Marcel keeps the date in both files and adds a note: one event can lift one reputation while wrecking another.
examples.whyItMatters: The audit makes hindsight less tidy. When the same branch crowns and ruins people, a clean moral story deserves suspicion.

examples.title: Unowned Result
examples.scenario: Simon had already cut the position, so the angry part of his mind needed a new target. Bad trader. Bad read. Bad nerve. He stopped at Stoicism in his note, then underlined fortune and external outcomes. The price move was not a vote on his worth. The size, the exit rule, and the boast he nearly posted were his. The loss could teach without owning him.
examples.whatToDo: Simon writes three lines in his notebook: exposure chosen, rule followed, story refused. He studies the first two and leaves the third alone.
examples.whyItMatters: Stoic distance is not numbness. It keeps the person close to the controllable parts and away from false self-punishment.

examples.title: Ruin Floor Cards
examples.scenario: Tatum spreads three index cards under a sticky note on the fridge: cash, reputation, sleep. The product launch has not begun, and no one has spent the ad money yet. She keeps thinking of Antony at Actium: one branch should not own the whole story. The attractive plan would look heroic if demand spikes. The quieter plan leaves more runway, fewer public claims, and less glory.
examples.whatToDo: Tatum writes the worst survivable loss on each card before picking any launch plan, then crosses out the claims that would make retreat humiliating.
examples.whyItMatters: The move sets a floor before luck acts. Dignity is easier when a bad branch was not allowed to become total ruin.

examples.title: Deleted Victory Post
examples.scenario: The victory post was gone before the client thread loaded. During the Friday dinner rush outside a delivery-app pickup zone, strategist Chase reread the client text thread after the campaign failed in public. The dilemma was ugly. Chase was torn between defending the old boast and blaming noise, or admitting the boast had outrun the exposure. Mark Antony after the Battle of Actium no longer felt ancient. It felt like a chat with receipts.
examples.whatToDo: Chase sends the shorter update: the process had a real edge, the exposure was too large, and the next plan will cap the bad branch first.
examples.whyItMatters: Candor costs status, but it protects judgment. The reader sees how to meet reversal without pretending the earlier applause proved control.

questions.prompt: Finley leaves the Actium seminar thinking Bacchus leaving Antony is only a dramatic ending. Which reading should replace that first reaction?
choices: The image mainly gives the scene a dramatic close, while the practical lesson sits elsewhere.
The image points to exposure, conduct, and the need not to let outcomes own the self.
The image shows that powerful people should accept whatever happens without planning.
questions.explanation: Dignified exposure is the mechanism. Antony's image opens the door, but the lesson is to avoid ruin, expect reversal, and keep the self from being owned by one result.

questions.prompt: A log shows five winning trades, then one loss that erases the gains. Which inference should Glenn make before judging the process?
choices: He should inspect the exposure and unseen bad branch before treating the streak as proof.
He should judge the method by the last result because it is the freshest evidence.
He should call the first five trades skill and the final trade bad luck.
questions.explanation: A sane stance checks the payoff shape and hidden alternatives. The latest result alone is not enough, and splitting wins into skill and losses into luck is too convenient.

questions.prompt: Simon reviews a trade log with repeated rewards and wants to raise the same large position. What does Antony after Actium warn him to notice?
choices: Rewards make an exposure safer each time they repeat.
Rewards matter only when a public reputation grows from them.
Rewards can arrive before the branch that reveals the real cost.
questions.explanation: Antony's fall shows how fast fortune can leave. Repeated reward may only mean the harmful state has not appeared yet, not that the exposure was safe.

questions.prompt: Two traders face the same loss: one attacks himself, the other reviews size, exit rule, and luck. Which response fits Stoic posture?
choices: The second response, because it separates controllable conduct from an outcome not fully under control.
The first response, because pain proves the trader is taking responsibility for the result.
Neither response, because Stoic practice treats all market outcomes as unworthy of review.
questions.explanation: Stoic distance is not skipping review. It keeps emotional ownership away from outcomes chance helped choose while still examining the choices that were his.

questions.prompt: Tatum can chase a launch plan with big upside and a ruinous bad branch. Why is this a moral risk question, not only a math question?
choices: The exposure choice shapes who gets hurt and how much life the reversal can damage.
The visible win would prove the team deserved the public praise it received.
The feeling of excitement is the best guide to whether the bet is sound.
questions.explanation: Exposure choices decide how reversal lands on people, promises, and future options. Observed success or excitement can hide the missing bad branch.

questions.prompt: Two founders compare plans: one seeks the highest public win, the other keeps habits that survive a cold market. Which preference fits dignified exposure?
choices: The public-win plan, because reputation is the cleanest record of skill.
The robust-habit plan, because ranking sees outcomes before it sees the risks behind them.
Either plan, because survival and applause carry the same evidence once the quarter closes.
questions.explanation: Dignified exposure favors robust habits over maximum visible success. Reputation often arrives after lucky timing and may miss the exposure that produced it.

questions.prompt: Marcel finds a polished story explaining why Octavian had to win and Antony had to fall. What should he distrust first?
choices: The use of Roman names, because old cases cannot teach modern risk.
The focus on one battle, because examples are only decoration.
The fitted story, because chance can be made to look causal after the result is known.
questions.explanation: The final discipline is posture toward reversal, not perfect prediction. A clean story after the fact can be built around the known outcome.

questions.prompt: Chase receives applause during a lucky state, then a reversal exposes a weak process. Which measure should carry more weight?
choices: The applause, because it records what observers knew at the time.
The process, restraint, and prep, because they travel better than praise when fortune turns.
The reversal, because the final feeling is the most honest risk report.
questions.explanation: Dignity comes from process, restraint, and preparedness. Applause and regret are vivid, but both can miss exposure, sample, and payoff shape.

questions.prompt: After Chase's public reversal, a teammate says the lesson is simply to accept defeat with style. Which answer names the surface reading to reject?
choices: It says reversal calls for better exposure choices before it calls for graceful language.
It says emotional acceptance belongs beside concrete limits on preventable ruin.
It says the main lesson is romantic resignation after fortune has withdrawn.
questions.explanation: The stem asks for the surface reading. Romantic resignation is the tempting simplification; the hard lesson joins acceptance to active restraint before ruin arrives.

reviewCards.front: What does dignified exposure ask you to do before fortune turns?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to cap preventable ruin, check the shape of the bet, and keep your self-respect from depending on the lucky branch staying lucky.

reviewCards.front: Why does Mark Antony after the Battle of Actium make reversal easy to remember?
reviewCards.back: In 31 BCE, a favored leader ended up on the losing side of Actium. The scene makes praise, status, and confidence feel reversible.

reviewCards.front: How can Octavian's victory and Cleopatra's collapse point to the same warning?
reviewCards.back: Octavian's victory helped shape Roman Empire power while Antony and Cleopatra collapsed. That split warns against reading the winner as pure skill and the loser as pure flaw.

reviewCards.front: What does Stoicism add when fortune moves external outcomes?
reviewCards.back: Stoicism adds emotional distance from external outcomes that fortune helped choose. You still review your choices, but you do not let a random result own your worth.

reviewCards.front: In one sentence, connect superstitious reinforcement (Ch 12) to dignified exposure: what should lucky feedback make you check?
reviewCards.back: Superstitious reinforcement warns that luck can train false confidence; dignified exposure answers by checking the exposure before lucky feedback becomes identity.

reviewCards.front: What wrong comfort should dignified exposure reject?
reviewCards.back: It rejects romantic resignation. The calmer face after a loss is not enough; the harder work is limiting preventable ruin before the loss arrives.

implementationPlan.title: Set the Ruin Floor
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice setting a floor under any choice that luck can punish. Set the Ruin Floor by naming the worst survivable loss, reducing any stake that would define you, and keeping your review focused on process. The skill is not fear; it is restraint before chance speaks.

ifThenPlans.context: A fresh win makes the whole plan feel smarter than it felt before.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a win starts proving too much, then Set the Ruin Floor by writing what the same exposure would have cost on a bad branch.

ifThenPlans.context: Repeated rewards make a large risk feel normal.
ifThenPlans.plan: If repetition starts sounding like safety, then Set the Ruin Floor by naming the adverse state that has not appeared yet.

ifThenPlans.context: A loss turns into a verdict about your worth.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the result starts judging you, then Set the Ruin Floor by separating the outcome, the exposure you chose, and the rule you followed.

ifThenPlans.context: Applause during a lucky state makes restraint feel unnecessary.
ifThenPlans.plan: If praise makes the stake grow, then Set the Ruin Floor by cutting one boast, debt, or promise that would make reversal humiliating.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, stage one rehearsal with a recent miss. On one sheet, draw boxes for result, exposure, and process, then point to each as you speak one sentence.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, rehearse a coming choice under real conditions. Before acting, write the worst survivable loss and physically cross out one stake that exceeds it.
